definition: Of only ordinary quality; not very good and often disappointing.
example: The movie had a mediocre script but a wonderful soundtrack.
nuance: Mediocre is harsher than average: it suggests that something falls short of what it should be, not just that it sits in the middle.
prompt: A food critic writes a review of the pancakes at a new diner.
options: She called the pancakes mediocre: edible, but bland and forgettable.
She called the pancakes mediocre because they were the finest she had ever tasted.
She ordered a mediocre stack, bigger than the small but smaller than the large.
She urged readers to drive across the state just for the mediocre pancakes.
reasons: Food that is acceptable yet dull and unmemorable fits the word's meaning of disappointing ordinariness.
The finest pancakes ever tasted would be outstanding, which is the reverse of this word.
This confuses the word with medium; it describes quality, not portion size.
Nobody makes a long trip for food that is only so-so, so the praise contradicts the word.

practice.prompt: A swim coach looks back on one athlete's season.
options: The coach served as a mediocre when two swimmers argued over lane assignments.
Teammates admired how mediocre she stayed, never bragging about a single win.
Her times were mediocre this year, nowhere near the speed she showed last spring.
Her mediocre times broke three school records and earned her a scholarship.
reasons: This mixes the word up with mediator; it is an adjective about quality, not a person who settles disputes.
This confuses the word with modest; it criticizes quality and does not describe humility.
Results that are unimpressive and below her own standard are exactly what the word describes.
Breaking records shows excellence, the opposite of merely ordinary performance.
